title: Gibbs Free Energy & Spontaneity
subtitle: The single number that decides if a reaction will go
subject: Chemistry
syllabusDotPoints: Apply the Gibbs free energy equation ΔG = ΔH − TΔS to predict spontaneity of a reaction at a given temperature
Calculate the temperature at which a reaction switches between spontaneous and non-spontaneous
lessonIntent: Students can calculate ΔG° from ΔH° and ΔS° at a given temperature, predict spontaneity from its sign, and find T at which ΔG° = 0.
examSkill: Convert ΔS° to kJ before substituting, apply ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, interpret sign for spontaneity, and find T_cross = ΔH°/ΔS°.
productionNotes: Mirrors site lesson `subjects/chemistry/year11/module4/lesson13.html`. Worked example: Haber Gibbs (verbatim), ΔH=−92.4 kJ/mol, ΔS=−198.9 J/K/mol = −0.1989 kJ/K/mol. T=298K: ΔG=−92.4−(298×−0.1989) = −33.1 kJ/mol (spontaneous). T_cross=−92.4/−0.1989=464.6K. T=773K: ΔG=+61.4 kJ/mol (non-spontaneous). Misconception (verbatim): 'negative ΔG means it happens quickly' (it means thermodynamically spontaneous; says NOTHING about rate). Module climax: ties ΔH (L1) + ΔS (L11-12) together.

voiceover.text: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity. Year eleven Chemistry, Module four.

scenes.heading: Will the reaction actually happen?
scenes.body: We've calculated ΔH (the energy change) and ΔS (the disorder change). But neither alone tells you whether a reaction will spontaneously go. That's what Gibbs free energy is for, one number that combines them.

bullets.text: ΔH alone isn't enough, endothermic reactions can be spontaneous.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS combines them with temperature.
Negative ΔG → reaction is spontaneous. That's the test.

scenes.callout: ΔG combines ΔH and ΔS into one go/no-go answer.
scenes.caption: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, the spontaneity test.

voiceover.text: Here's the climax of Module four. You've calculated delta H — the energy change. You've calculated delta S — the disorder change. But neither alone tells you whether a reaction will actually go. Think of delta H and delta S like two votes on whether to start a project — you need both, weighted by some criterion, to make the final call. But unlike a vote with equal weights, the weighting here is temperature — and that's exactly what Gibbs free energy does. Delta G combines them: negative means go.

scenes.heading: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°
scenes.body: One equation. Three quantities you've already calculated. One critical unit gotcha.

bullets.text: T is absolute temperature, in kelvin (add 273 to °C).
Unit gotcha: ΔS° in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, convert to kJ first.
ΔG° predicts the standard-state tendency; actual direction depends on ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q.

scenes.callout: Convert ΔS° to kJ before substituting (divide by 1000).
scenes.caption: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°. T in kelvin; ΔS° in kJ.

voiceover.text: One equation does it all. Delta G zero equals delta H zero minus T delta S zero. T is absolute temperature, in kelvin — so add two-seventy-three to anything given in Celsius. The unit gotcha is critical: delta S zero from last lesson is in joules per kelvin per mole, but delta H is in kilojoules. You must convert delta S to kilojoules first, by dividing by one thousand. Skip that and your answer is off by a factor of a thousand. For actual delta G, negative favours the forward direction; delta G zero is the standard value and actual delta G also includes R T log Q.

scenes.heading: Haber process: spontaneity and crossover temperature
scenes.question: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH° = −92.4 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = −198.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate ΔG° at 25 °C. (b) Is the reaction forward-favoured in the standard state at 25 °C? (c) Find the temperature where ΔG° = 0.
scenes.coachNote: Convert ΔS to kJ first. Convert T to K. Then substitute carefully, watch the double-negative.
steps: Known: ΔH° = −92.4 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS° = −198.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Find: (a) ΔG° at 298 K, (b) spontaneity, (c) crossover T.
Convert: T = 25 + 273 = 298 K; ΔS° = −0.1989 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
(b) ΔG° is negative → forward-favoured in the standard state at 25 °C.
scenes.caption: ΔG°(298 K) = −33.1 kJ mol⁻¹ (spontaneous); T_cross ≈ 465 K.

voiceover.text: The Haber process at room temperature. Delta H is minus ninety-two-point-four kilojoules per mole. Delta S is minus one-ninety-eight-point-nine joules per kelvin per mole. First, convert: temperature is twenty-five plus two-seventy-three, two-ninety-eight kelvin. Delta S in kilojoules is minus zero-point-one-nine-eight-nine. Now substitute: delta G equals minus ninety-two-point-four minus two-ninety-eight times minus zero-point-one-nine-eight-nine. Watch the double negative — that's minus ninety-two-point-four minus negative fifty-nine-point-two-seven, which is minus ninety-two-point-four plus fifty-nine-point-two-seven, giving minus thirty-three-point-one kilojoules per mole. Negative — so spontaneous at room temperature. For the crossover temperature, set delta G to zero: T equals delta H over delta S, both negatives cancel, giving four hundred and sixty-five kelvin — about one hundred and ninety-two Celsius. Above that, delta G turns positive. This uses the standard-state free-energy change. Actual direction depends on composition through Q. The crossover estimate assumes enthalpy and entropy changes remain approximately constant with temperature; ΔG nought equals zero corresponds to K equals one.

scenes.heading: "Negative ΔG means the reaction is fast"
scenes.body: Students often think: "ΔG is negative, so the reaction will happen quickly." That's the wrong instinct, and it confuses thermodynamics with kinetics. The correct rule: a negative ΔG means the reaction is thermodynamically spontaneous, it CAN occur without external energy. It says nothing about rate. The Haber process is forward-favoured in the standard state at 25 °C but essentially no reaction happens, kinetics, not thermodynamics, limit it.
scenes.callout: Negative ΔG = thermodynamically allowed. Rate is a separate question.
scenes.caption: Negative ΔG means thermodynamically spontaneous, rate is a separate question.

scenes.question: For C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g), ΔH° = −137 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = −120.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔG° at 25 °C and decide whether the reaction is spontaneous.

answerSteps: Convert: T = 298 K; ΔS° = −0.1207 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Answer: ΔG° = 101 kJ mol⁻¹ released (i.e. −101 kJ mol⁻¹) → forward-favoured in the standard state at 25 °C.

voiceover.text: Your turn. Hydrogenation of ethene. Delta H is minus one-thirty-seven, delta S is minus one-twenty-point-seven joules per kelvin per mole. Find delta G at twenty-five degrees and decide. Pause and try. T is two-ninety-eight kelvin. Delta S in kilojoules is minus zero-point-one-two-zero-seven. Delta G equals minus one-thirty-seven minus two-ninety-eight times minus zero-point-one-two-zero-seven — minus one-thirty-seven minus minus thirty-five-point-nine-seven — which is minus one-thirty-seven plus thirty-five-point-nine-seven, giving minus one-hundred-and-one kilojoules per mole. Negative standard delta G — product-favoured at twenty-five degrees; actual direction depends on reaction composition.

scenes.heading: Summary
scenes.finalPrompt: Always check the sign of ΔG: negative means spontaneous, never fast.
points: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, combines enthalpy and entropy at temperature T.
Convert ΔS° to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ before substituting (it's the most common error).
Negative ΔG° → thermodynamically spontaneous; positive → non-spontaneous.
Spontaneous ≠ fast, rate is a separate (kinetic) question.
scenes.caption: One equation, three quantities, one decision rule.

voiceover.text: Five takeaways for the module climax. One: delta G zero equals delta H zero minus T delta S zero — it combines enthalpy and entropy at a given temperature. Two: convert delta S to kilojoules per kelvin per mole before substituting, by dividing by one thousand — this is the most common error. Three: T is absolute, in kelvin — add two-seventy-three to Celsius. Four: negative delta G means thermodynamically spontaneous; positive means non-spontaneous. Five: spontaneous is not the same as fast — rate is a separate, kinetic question. Decision rule: check the sign of delta G — negative means spontaneous, never automatically fast.
